subject: Computer Networking
title: SPF — Sender Verification
description: A short lesson to help you apply SPF — Sender Verification.

hook.text: Anyone can write any From address in an email. SPF is the first check that catches the liars.

buildup.text: SPF — Sender Policy Framework — is a DNS record listing IPs allowed to send for a domain.

discovery.text: The receiving server checks: did this email come from an IP listed in the sender's SPF record?

twist.text: SPF breaks when email is forwarded. The forwarding server's IP isn't in the original domain's SPF record.

climax.text: SPF alone isn't enough. It checks the envelope sender, not the From header the user sees.

punchline.text: SPF asks: is this server allowed to send for this domain?

quiz.question: Where is a domain's SPF record published?
options: In DNS as a TXT record
In the SMTP server's config file

details.summary: Sender Policy Framework is a DNS-based email authentication method that specifies which servers are authorized to send email for a domain. Receiving servers check SPF records to verify that incoming mail actually comes from an authorized source, helping detect forged sender addresses.
details.whyItMatters: SPF is the first layer of email authentication. Without it, anyone can send email pretending to be from your domain. SPF does not stop all spoofing but makes basic forgery detectable.
takeaways: SPF publishes authorized sending servers in DNS TXT records
Receiving servers check if the sending IP matches the SPF record
SPF alone is insufficient; it works best with DKIM and DMARC

faq.question: How does an SPF check work?
faq.answer: When an email arrives, the receiving server extracts the sending domain from the envelope. It queries DNS for the domain's SPF record, which lists authorized IP addresses. If the sending server's IP matches, SPF passes. If not, the server can reject or flag the message.

faq.question: Why isn't SPF sufficient for email security?
faq.answer: SPF only checks the envelope sender, not the From header displayed to users. An attacker can use a legitimate envelope sender while spoofing the visible From address. DKIM adds cryptographic verification and DMARC ties SPF and DKIM to the visible domain.
